When can classical neural networks represent quantum states?

Tai-Hsuan Yang∗1,2,3 Affiliation: 1University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA    Mehdi Soleimanifar∗3 Affiliation: 1University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA    Thiago Bergamaschi4 Affiliation: 1University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA    John Preskill3,5 Affiliation: 1University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA Affiliation: 2National Taiwan University, Taipei City, Taiwan Affiliation: 3California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA Affiliation: 4University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA Affiliation: 5AWS Center for Quantum Computing, Pasadena, CA, USA Thanks: Co-first author.
Abstract

A naive classical representation of an nn-qubit state requires specifying exponentially many amplitudes in the computational basis. Past works have demonstrated that classical neural networks can succinctly express these amplitudes for many physically relevant states, leading to computationally powerful representations known as neural quantum states. What underpins the efficacy of such representations? We show that conditional correlations present in the measurement distribution of quantum states control the performance of their neural representations. Such conditional correlations are basis dependent, arise due to measurement-induced entanglement, and reveal features not accessible through conventional few-body correlations often examined in studies of phases of matter. By combining theoretical and numerical analysis, we demonstrate how the state’s entanglement and sign structure, along with the choice of measurement basis, give rise to distinct patterns of short- or long-range conditional correlations. Our findings provide a rigorous framework for exploring the expressive power of neural quantum states.

I Introduction

Modern machine learning (ML) algorithms based on artificial neural networks have achieved impressive results in image and language processing. Recent works have shown that similar architectures can also be employed to classically simulate the properties of many-body quantum systems [17, 50, 58, 22, 34, 51], or learn a classical representation of a quantum state from measurement data [18, 50, 69, 39, 75, 68]. To achieve this, a machine learning model such as a recurrent neural network [34, 35], convolutional neural network [22], or restricted Boltzmann machine [17] is used to concisely represent the amplitudes ψ⁡(x)=⟨x|ψ⟩\psi(x)=\left\langle x\middle|\psi\right\rangle of an nn-qubit state |ψ⟩=∑x∈{0,1}nψ(x)|x⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\psi(x)\left|x\right\rangle in some fixed basis. That is, upon querying with a bit string x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the ML model returns a complex value ψ⁡(x)\psi(x) that we interpret as the amplitude of a possibly un-normalized state |ψ⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle. The ML model admits a series of weights collectively denoted by ww. Each configuration of these weights ww, leads to the representation of a particular quantum state |ψw⟩\left|\psi_{w}\right\rangle. For such a representation to be useful, the set of weights and the running time of the ML model should scale at most polynomially poly⁡(n)\operatorname{poly}(n) with the number of qubits. Overall, this yields a parameterized family of nn-qubit states {|ψw⟩}\{\left|\psi_{w}\right\rangle\} referred to as neural quantum states [17].

The neural representation of quantum states provides a powerful computational and statistical model, allowing for sampling from the measurement distribution of the state [13, 12, 68], Monte Carlo estimation of sparse observables [17, 50, 58, 22, 34, 51], state certification with few single-qubit measurements [38], and dequantization of quantum algorithms [21, 66]. Despite their wide range of applications and empirical effectiveness, the theoretical underpinning of why neural networks could, in principle, be used to represent the many-body states of interest is not fully understood. Indeed at first sight, the practical success of neural quantum states seems in conflict with the fact that general nn-qubit states require exponentially many parameters to be precisely specified. However, in practice, the constraints imposed by the physics of the system may be leveraged to achieve an efficient classical representation of its state. A notable example of such constraints is the area law for entanglement entropy in gapped ground states, which underpins our understanding of tensor network representations of these states [31, 5, 3, 2, 4].

In this paper, we reveal a physical feature of quantum states that controls the efficiency of their neural representation. This property can be best introduced by considering a representation of the quantum state using recurrent neural networks (RNN) [34, 35, 51], although as we will see, our findings extend to other architectures. In the RNN representation of a quantum state, we express the amplitudes in polar form, ψ⁡(x)=|ψ⁡(x)|⋅ei​g​(x)\psi(x)=|\psi(x)|\cdot e^{ig(x)}, with the magnitude |ψ⁡(x)||\psi(x)| and phase ei​g​(x)e^{ig(x)} components treated separately. We focus primarily on the power and limitations of RNN in representing the magnitudes |ψ⁡(x)||\psi(x)|, setting aside the phase component ei​g​(x)e^{ig(x)}. This simplification incurs no loss of generality for the sign-free states considered in Section II.2. More broadly, as discussed in Section III, the presence of complex phases often hinders finding neural representations for quantum states—a challenge encountered across various simulation and learning applications [56, 25, 65, 15].

The squared-magnitudes p⁡(x):=|ψ⁡(x)|2p(x):=|\psi(x)|^{2} simply correspond to the distribution obtained by measuring the state |ψ⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle in the computational basis. The RNN representation of this distribution is based on the chain rule of probabilities

p(x1,…,xn)=p(x1)p(x2|x1)⋯p(xn|x1,…,xn−1).\displaystyle p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=p(x_{1})p(x_{2}|x_{1})\cdots p(x_{n}|x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}). (1)

Starting with p⁡(x1)p(x_{1}) and proceeding successively, each conditional probability p⁡(xk|x1,…,xk−1)p(x_{k}|x_{1},\dots,x_{k-1}) is computed by a feedforward neural network acting on x1,…,xk−1x_{1},\dots,x_{k-1} and a hidden state hk−1h_{k-1} from the last step, see Figure 1.

The conditional probability p⁡(xk|x1,…,xk−1)p(x_{k}|x_{1},\dots,x_{k-1}) for k≤nk\leq n could in general be a complicated kk-bit function with an exponential complexity 𝒪⁡(2k)\mathcal{O}(2^{k}). Hence, for the RNN to be able to efficiently compute these probabilities, we need to impose further conditions. A sufficient (though not necessary) criterion is conditional independence of the variables. That is, the distribution of each variable xkx_{k} is only dependent on the previous ℓ\ell variables xk−ℓ,…,xk−1x_{k-\ell},\dots,x_{k-1} for some ℓ∈[k−1]\ell\in[k-1] such that

p⁡(xk|x1,…,xk−1)=p⁡(xk|xk−ℓ,…,xk−1).\displaystyle p(x_{k}|x_{1},\dots,x_{k-1})=p(x_{k}|x_{k-\ell},\dots,x_{k-1}). (2)

This reduces the worst-case complexity of computing each conditional distribution to 𝒪⁡(2ℓ)\mathcal{O}(2^{\ell}), which can be polynomially-bounded for a sufficiently small ℓ≤𝒪⁡(log⁡n)\ell\leq\mathcal{O}(\log n), and leads to an efficient neural network representation as we show in Section II.

In fact, a similar argument applies even when the conditional independence in Eq. (2) only approximately holds. This is relevant because many quantum states of interest, such as those examined in Theorem II.2, are known to satisfy the approximate version. To quantify this, we use classical conditional mutual information I(𝖠:𝖢|𝖡)I(\mathsf{A}:\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}) as a measure of conditional correlations. This quantity represents the average correlation between two sets of variables, 𝖠\mathsf{A} and 𝖢\mathsf{C}, conditioned on the value of the variables in 𝖡\mathsf{B} (see Section II for a formal definition).

Altering the measurement basis can significantly affect the amount of conditional correlations, reflecting the basis-dependent nature of neural quantum states and our analysis throughout this work. This contrasts with ‘localizable entanglement’ [70, 59], which corresponds to the maximum entanglement that can be created on average between subsystems 𝖠\mathsf{A} and 𝖢\mathsf{C} through local measurements on the qubits in 𝖡\mathsf{B}. Conditional correlations are also distinct from conventional two-point (or bipartite) correlations, which are often used to characterize phases of matter or explain the success of classical simulation techniques. Quantum states with short-range two-point correlations can show either short- or long-range conditional correlations upon measurement (e.g., cluster state in the ZZ versus XX basis). Likewise, those with long-range two-point correlations can also display either type of conditional correlations (e.g., output states of deep quantum circuits versus quantum phase states [40, 10]).

Previous works have identified distinct computational and algebraic barriers that limit the (worst-case) expressiveness of neural quantum states [27, 37, 61, 41]. We will see that our information-theoretic approach, based on characterizing conditional correlations, provides a unified and physically tangible framework for studying these and more general obstacles to the neural representation of quantum states.

Motivated by these observations, we explore the presence or absence of conditional independence in the measurement distribution p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) of an nn-qubit quantum state, and how this influences both the existence and the computational tractability of finding an efficient neural representation. We consider quantum states that, roughly speaking, exhibit one of the following features:

  1. (1)

    The distribution p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) has short-range conditional correlations, corresponding to a small ℓ\ell in Eq. (2), and can be efficiently represented by shallow neural networks.

  2. (2)

    The distribution p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) exhibits long-range conditional correlations, but still allows for an efficient neural network representation. However, variationally finding such a representation (e.g., via gradient descent) may be challenging.

  3. (3)

    The distribution p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) has long-range conditional correlations that are difficult to represent with efficient neural networks.

We emphasize that this is a non-exhaustive list of the types of conditional correlations that can occur in quantum systems, and our work does not rule out many other possibilities. For instance, the conditional distributions in (2) may depend on a small number of variables ℓ\ell, which are not necessarily geometrically local. Alternatively, the conditional mutual information I(𝖠:𝖢|𝖡)I(\mathsf{A}:\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}) may decay, but not necessarily at an exponential rate. There might also exist efficiently trainable neural quantum states with long-range conditional correlations.

Through rigorous analysis and numerical experiments, we explore how each of the above cases (1), (2), and (3) arises in physically motivated states. We identify the amount of (pre-measurement) entanglement in the state, the sign structure of the amplitudes, and the local measurement basis as crucial factors determining the type of measurement-induced correlations in the state. Our results are summarized as follows:

Result 1. Quantum states with short-range conditional correlations admit shallow neural network representations.

We state this result more formally in Theorem II.2 and prove it in Appendix B.1.

Result 2. The ground states of prototypical gapped spin systems, states generated by random shallow 1D quantum circuits, and random tensor network states with predominantly positive tensor entries display short-range conditional correlations.

The setting of random shallow 1D quantum circuits is stated in Theorem II.3 and proved in Appendix D.6. Numerical evidence for spin systems and random tensor network states is presented in Section II.3 and Section II.2 respectively.

Result 3. The 1D cluster state, subjected to single-qubit rotations, exhibits conditional correlations that transition from short- to long-range as the rotation angle varies. This transition is accompanied by a decline in the performance of variational algorithms in finding the neural representation of the state.

The conditional correlations in cluster states are bounded in Theorem III.1, and the numerical evidence for the computational hardness of finding the rotated cluster state is discussed in Section III.1.

Lastly, in Section III.2, we discuss how recent studies on random 2D tensor networks and states prepared by random 2D shallow quantum circuits suggest that the proliferation of long-range correlations induced by measurements poses a significant obstacle to efficiently representing these states with neural networks.

While our primary focus is on neural representations of quantum states and the Monte Carlo algorithms based on them, our work lies within the broader context of measurement-induced entanglement and monitored quantum circuits, which have been the subject of much interest in relation to phases of many-body entanglement [45, 62, 19, 6, 1, 59], classical simulation of random quantum circuits [54, 7], and probing the sign problem [32, 46].

II Short-range conditional correlations

We consider an entangled system of qubits arranged on the vertices of a finite-dimensional lattice such as a one-dimensional chain or two-dimensional grid. Consider three subsets of qubits 𝖠\mathsf{A}, 𝖡\mathsf{B}, and 𝖢\mathsf{C} where 𝖠∪𝖡∪𝖢⊆[n]\mathsf{A}\cup\mathsf{B}\cup\mathsf{C}\subseteq[n], with dist⁡(𝖠,𝖢)\mathrm{dist}(\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C}) denoting the length of the shortest path connecting 𝖠\mathsf{A} and 𝖡\mathsf{B} on the lattice. Suppose when the qubits in the subset 𝖡\mathsf{B} are measured in the computational basis, we observe the outcome x𝖡∈{0,1}|𝖡|{x}_{\mathsf{B}}\in\{0,1\}^{|\mathsf{B}|}. We let p𝖠,𝖢|𝖡​(x𝖠,x𝖢|x𝖡)p_{\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}}(x_{\mathsf{A}},x_{\mathsf{C}}|{x}_{\mathsf{B}}) denote the marginal distribution of measurement outcomes for qubits in 𝖠\mathsf{A} and 𝖢\mathsf{C} conditioned on observing xB{x}_{B}. The marginal distributions p𝖠|𝖡​(x𝖠|x𝖡)p_{\mathsf{A}|\mathsf{B}}(x_{\mathsf{A}}|{x}_{\mathsf{B}}) and p𝖢|𝖡​(x𝖢|x𝖡)p_{\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}}(x_{\mathsf{C}}|{x}_{\mathsf{B}}) are defined in a similar way. We say the measurement outcomes in regions 𝖠\mathsf{A} and 𝖢\mathsf{C} are conditionally independent with respect to the outcomes in region 𝖡\mathsf{B} when for any x𝖡x_{\mathsf{B}} such that p𝖡​(x𝖡)>0p_{\mathsf{B}}(x_{\mathsf{B}})>0 and any choices of x𝖠x_{\mathsf{A}} and x𝖢x_{\mathsf{C}}, we have

p𝖠,𝖢|𝖡​(x𝖠,x𝖢|x𝖡)=p𝖠|𝖡​(x𝖠|x𝖡)​p𝖢|𝖡​(x𝖢|x𝖡).\displaystyle p_{\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}}(x_{\mathsf{A}},x_{\mathsf{C}}|{x}_{\mathsf{B}})=p_{\mathsf{A}|\mathsf{B}}(x_{\mathsf{A}}|{x}_{\mathsf{B}})p_{\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}}(x_{\mathsf{C}}|{x}_{\mathsf{B}}).

A stronger notion of conditional independence is captured using the classical conditional mutual information (CMI) defined by

I(𝖠:𝖢|𝖡):=𝔼𝖡DKL(p𝖠,𝖢|𝖡∥p𝖠|𝖡⊗p𝖢|𝖡),\displaystyle I(\mathsf{A}:\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}):=\mathbb{E\/}_{\mathsf{B}}D_{\text{KL}}(p_{\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}}\parallel p_{\mathsf{A}|\mathsf{B}}\otimes p_{\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}}), (3)

where the expectation is over x𝖡∼p𝖡​(x𝖡)x_{\mathsf{B}}\sim p_{\mathsf{B}}(x_{\mathsf{B}}) and the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between two distributions qq and q′q^{\prime} is given by DKL(q∥q′)=𝔼x∼qlog(q(x)/q′(x))D_{\text{KL}}(q\parallel q^{\prime})=\mathbb{E\/}_{{x}\sim q}\log\left({q({x})/q^{\prime}({x})}\right) in their support. These two notions are connected by 𝔼𝖡||p𝖠,𝖢|𝖡−p𝖠|𝖡⊗p𝖢|𝖡||1≤2⋅I(𝖠:𝖢|𝖡)\mathbb{E\/}_{\mathsf{B}}{\big|\hskip-1.59016pt\big|p_{\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}}-p_{\mathsf{A}|\mathsf{B}}\otimes p_{\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}}\big|\hskip-1.59016pt\big|}_{1}\leq\sqrt{2\cdot I(\mathsf{A}:\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B})}, which follows from the well-known Pinsker’s inequality.

Quantum states with short-range conditional correlations may exhibit an approximate version of conditional independence defined as follows:

Definition II.1 (Approximate conditional independence in measurement distribution).

The probability distribution obtained by measuring an nn-qubit quantum state |ψ⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle in the computational basis satisfies the approximate conditional independence with respect to subsets 𝖠∪𝖡∪𝖢⊆[n]\mathsf{A}\cup\mathsf{B}\cup\mathsf{C}\subseteq[n], if there is a constant ξ\xi and a function α⁡(𝖠,𝖢)\alpha(\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C}) such that

I(𝖠:𝖢|𝖡)≤α(𝖠,𝖢)⋅e−dist(𝖠,𝖢)/ξ.\displaystyle I(\mathsf{A}:\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B})\leq\alpha({\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C}})\cdot e^{-\mathrm{dist}(\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C})/\xi}. (4)

and α⁡(𝖠,𝖢)≤poly⁡(|𝖠|,|𝖢|)\alpha({\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C}})\leq\operatorname{poly}(|\mathsf{A}|,|\mathsf{C}|). We refer to parameter ξ\xi as the CMI length.

Based on Definition II.1, we classify conditional correlations as long-range under two circumstances: (1) the conditional mutual information (CMI) does not decay exponentially as in (4); or (2) for a fixed number of qubits, as a Hamiltonian parameter (e.g., the rotation angle in Section III.1) is varied, the CMI length ξ\xi increases and becomes comparable to the size of the lattice. Otherwise, we describe the conditional correlations as being short-range.

To connect this notion of approximate conditional independence to efficient neural network representation of the state |ψ⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle, we consider two architectures for neural quantum states, depicted in Figure 1 and introduced formally in Appendix A.1. The first is the feedforward neural network. This architecture consists of a network of neurons, each of which applies an affine transformation to its input followed by a non-linear activation function. The number of layers in the network is referred to as the depth, while the maximum number of neurons in any layer is known as the width of the neural network. As discussed in Section I, we also consider recurrent neural networks (RNN), which compute the probabilities p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) via the chain rule stated in Eq. (1). An RNN consists of a cascade of cells, functioning as feedforward neural networks. The kkth cell processes an input bit xkx_{k} and a hidden memory state hkh_{k}. The number of neurons in each cell and the size of the memory determine the complexity of evaluating an RNN.

We now state our first result which applies the conditional independence property Definition II.1 in a quantum state to construct its neural representation. The proof is given in Appendix B.1.

Theorem II.2 (Neural quantum state from conditional independence).

Consider nn qubits arranged on a DΛD_{\Lambda}-dimensional lattice Λ\Lambda with a quantum state |ψ⟩=∑x∈{0,1}nψ(x)|x⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\psi(x)\left|x\right\rangle. Suppose the measurement distribution p⁡(x)=|ψ⁡(x)|2p(x)=|\psi(x)|^{2} in this basis satisfies the approximate conditional independence property given in Definition II.1 with respect to geometrically contiguous regions shown in Figure 2. Then, there exists a feedforward neural network with

depth=𝒪⁡(log⁡log⁡(n))​ and width=n𝒪⁡(logDΛ−1⁡(n))\displaystyle\text{depth}=\mathcal{O}\left(\log\log(n)\right)\text{ \ and width}=n^{\mathcal{O}(\log^{D_{\Lambda}-1}(n))} (5)

that computes a function q⁡(x)q(x) such that ∑x|q⁡(x)−p⁡(x)|≤1/poly⁡(n)\sum_{x}|q(x)-p(x)|\leq 1/\operatorname{poly}(n). This can also be achieved using a recurrent neural network with DΛD_{\Lambda}-dimensional geometry, a memory size of 𝒪⁡(logDΛ⁡(n))\mathcal{O}(\log^{D_{\Lambda}}(n)), and feedforward cells with width and depth given by (5).

While Theorem II.2 guarantees the existence of a shallow neural network representation for magnitudes |ψ⁡(x)||\psi(x)| of states with short-range conditional correlations, it does not imply that statistically learning such a representation is easy. This can be illustrated with quantum phase states of the form |ψ⟩=∑x∈{0,1}n12nei​g​(x)|x⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^{n}}}e^{ig(x)}\left|x\right\rangle, which exhibit no conditional correlations. However, for a random choice of phases g⁡(x)g(x), these states can be highly entangled and indistinguishable from Haar random states [40, 10].

The proof of Theorem II.2 follows strategies similar to those employed in several previous works [11, 54, 7, 32, 60]. The decay of quantum conditional mutual information is used in [11] to prepare the Gibbs state of a quantum state. Conditions similar to Definition II.1 form the basis for the classical algorithms in [54, 7] for simulating the measurement distribution of shallow random quantum circuits, as well as the “coherent Gibbs state” representation of non-negative wavefunctions in [32]. We emphasize that our use of conditional independence is limited to geometrically contiguous regions 𝖠,𝖡,𝖢⊂[n]\mathsf{A},\mathsf{B},\mathsf{C}\subset[n], while [54, 11] consider regions distributed non-locally on the lattice. There are examples of quantum states such as cluster states [76] where conditional independence holds for geometrically local regions but not for arbitrary subsets of qubits.

In light of Theorem II.2, we seek to identify processes in quantum systems that lead to short-range conditional correlations, as described in Definition II.1. We discuss two such mechanisms in what follows: (1) sufficiently low amount of entanglement in the state prior to subsystem measurements, and (2) non-negative amplitudes ψ⁡(x)≥0\psi(x)\geq 0 corresponding to a sign-free (also known as stoquastic) state |ψ⟩=∑x∈{0,1}nψ(x)|x⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\psi(x)\left|x\right\rangle. Additionally, in Section III, we demonstrate how the choice of measurement basis can alter the range of conditional correlations.

II.1 Sufficiently low entanglement

The amount and structure of entanglement in a quantum state affect the conditional correlations in its measurement distribution. This is most evident when the state |ψ⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle is generated by a low-depth quantum circuit. When this shallow circuit has a one-dimensional geometry, the study of conditional correlations effectively reduces to analyzing an entanglement swapping setup. In its simplest form, as defined in Definition D.5, entanglement swapping refers to the formation of a maximally entangled state between the subsystems 𝖫i\mathsf{L}_{i} and 𝖱i+1\mathsf{R}_{i+1} of a four-qubit state |EPR⟩𝖫i​𝖱i⊗|EPR⟩𝖫i+1​𝖱i+1\left|\mathrm{EPR}\right\rangle_{\mathsf{L}_{i}\mathsf{R}_{i}}\otimes\left|\mathrm{EPR}\right\rangle_{\mathsf{L}_{i+1}\mathsf{R}_{i+1}} when subsystems 𝖱i\mathsf{R}_{i} and 𝖫i+1\mathsf{L}_{i+1} are jointly measured in the Bell basis. Such a Bell basis measurement is equivalent to applying an entangling gate followed by single-qubit measurements. Now consider a one-dimensional circuit of constant depth DD with the brickwork architecture consisting of alternating layers of two-qubit gates as in Figure 3(a). The effect of computational-basis measurements on the output state of this depth-DD circuit can be understood as consecutive applications of entanglement swapping measurements. To illustrate this, we first partition the gates into disjoint groups: ’backward lightcones’ in green and ’forward lightcones’ in orange, as shown in Figure 3. We then replace |EPR⟩⊗|EPR⟩\left|\mathrm{EPR}\right\rangle\otimes\left|\mathrm{EPR}\right\rangle in the previous setup with the state

|ai⟩𝖫i​𝖱i⊗|ai+1⟩𝖫i+1​𝖱i+1=\displaystyle\left|a_{i}\right\rangle_{\mathsf{L}_{i}\mathsf{R}_{i}}\otimes\left|a_{i+1}\right\rangle_{\mathsf{L}_{i+1}\mathsf{R}_{i+1}}=\raisebox{-0.5pt}{\includegraphics[height=51.6665pt]{es3.png}} (6)

prepared by applying the gates in the backward lightcones on |0⟩𝖫i​𝖱i⊗|0⟩𝖫i+1​𝖱i+1\left|0\right\rangle_{\mathsf{L}_{i}\mathsf{R}_{i}}\otimes\left|0\right\rangle_{\mathsf{L}_{i+1}\mathsf{R}_{i+1}} with 𝖫𝗂\mathsf{L_{i}}, 𝖱i\mathsf{R}_{i}, 𝖫i+1\mathsf{L}_{i+1}, and 𝖱i+1\mathsf{R}_{i+1}being subsystems of D−1D-1 qubits. Finally, instead of Bell basis measurements, we perform entangling measurements by applying the gates in the forward lightcone on subsystems 𝖱i\mathsf{R}_{i} and 𝖫i+1\mathsf{L}_{i+1}, followed by computational basis measurements on these subsystems. The post-measurement state is given by

(7)

and can exhibit entanglement between disjoint subsystems 𝖫i\mathsf{L}_{i} and 𝖱i+1\mathsf{R}_{i+1} analogous to entanglement swapping with EPR pairs. Measurements throughout the circuit induce multiple rounds of entanglement swapping, ultimately allowing distant parts of the circuit to become entangled. This process is illustrated in Figure 3(b) for a small circuit consisting of six subsystems.

As we will see in Appendix D.2, by carefully choosing the gates in the circuit, one can always implement a perfect entanglement swapping in which the initial states and joint measurements are maximally entangled. This leads to the formation of long-range measurement-induced entanglement between distant subsystems. However, for typical circuits where the gates are not fine-tuned and instead randomly chosen, this is no longer the case. For such random sufficiently-shallow circuits, we expect the states and joint measurements to only be partially entangled. In Appendix D.6, we show that in this case, each round of measurements reduces the post-measurement entanglement by a constant factor, leading to an overall exponential decay in measurement-induced entanglement and conditional correlations between distant subsystems. As the following theorem states, this decay ensures that conditional correlations between regions of length Ω⁡(log⁡(n))\Omega(\log(n)) are negligibly small.

Theorem II.3 (Conditional independence in random shallow 1D circuits).

Consider the family of random depth-DD brickwork quantum circuits acting on a one-dimensional chain of qudits with local dimension dd. Fix L≥c0⋅(4​d)3​D⋅log⁡(n⋅D​log⁡(d))L\geq c_{0}\cdot(4d)^{3D}\cdot\log(n\cdot D\log(d)) for some sufficiently large constant c0c_{0} and define contiguous regions 𝖠1∪⋯∪𝖠n′\mathsf{A}_{1}\cup\dots\cup\mathsf{A}_{n^{\prime}} from left to right with n′=n/Ln^{\prime}=n/L such that the size of each region is |𝖠i|=L≥Ω⁡(log⁡(n))|\mathsf{A}_{i}|=L\geq\Omega(\log(n)) and dist⁡(𝖠i−𝖠j)≥Ω⁡(log⁡(n))\mathrm{dist}(\mathsf{A}_{i}-\mathsf{A}_{j})\geq\Omega(\log(n)) for |i−j|>1|i-j|>1. With probability 1−1/poly⁡(n)1-1/\operatorname{poly}(n) over the random choice of circuits, the measurement distribution of these random circuits satisfies the conditional independence property

I(𝖠i:𝖠j|𝖠i+1,…,𝖠j−1)≤e−Ω⁡(dist⁡(𝖠i,𝖠j))≤1/poly(n).\displaystyle I(\mathsf{A}_{i}:\mathsf{A}_{j}|\mathsf{A}_{i+1},\dots,\mathsf{A}_{j-1})\leq e^{-\Omega{\left(\mathrm{dist}(\mathsf{A}_{i},\mathsf{A}_{j})\right)}}\leq 1/\operatorname{poly}(n).

for any 1≤i<j≤n′1\leq i<j\leq n^{\prime} with |i−j|>1|i-j|>1.

Going beyond the 1D architecture, random shallow quantum circuits with a 2D geometry have also been conjectured and numerically shown to exhibit short-range conditional independence [54, 6, 7, 47] for depths smaller than a critical constant value. Similar behavior has been observed in random 2D tensor networks, known as projected entangled pair states (PEPS) [28]. When the bond dimension of these states is sufficiently small, the boundary entanglement of contracted PEPS follows an area law, indicating that the amplitudes of the state can be efficiently determined via tensor contraction methods. In all these cases, however, a phase transition occurs beyond a small critical depth or bond dimension, where the conditional correlations become long-range. We defer a more detailed discussion of this transition to Section III.

The properties of structured, physically relevant states may differ from those generated by random ensembles of quantum circuits and tensor networks [28]. To further support our findings, we next investigate the correlations in a class of physically motivated, sign-free local Hamiltonians. Following this, in Section II.3, we perform a numerical investigation of conditional correlations in several well-studied spin systems.

II.2 Non-negative amplitudes

Another property of a many-body quantum state that can affect conditional independence in its measurement distribution is the sign structure of its amplitudes. A wide class of commonly studied local Hamiltonians enjoy the feature that their off-diagonal terms are non-positive. That is, in a local basis {|x⟩:x∈{0,1}n}\{\left|x\right\rangle:x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\}, we have

⟨x|H|y⟩≤0forx≠y.\displaystyle\left\langle x\right|H\left|y\right\rangle\leq 0\quad\text{for}\quad x\neq y. (8)

Such Hamiltonians are called sign-free or “stoquastic”. The (unique) ground state of a sign-free Hamiltonian is a quantum state |ψ⟩=∑xψ(x)|x⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle=\sum_{x}\psi(x)\left|x\right\rangle with non-negative amplitudes ψ⁡(x)≥0\psi(x)\geq 0.

In the absence of topological order, the non-negativity of the amplitudes can constrain the amount of post-measurement entanglement that can be formed in the state. This, for instance, may be seen in the entanglement swapping setup introduced earlier. Although the initial state |EPR⟩⊗|EPR⟩\left|\mathrm{EPR}\right\rangle\otimes\left|\mathrm{EPR}\right\rangle is non-negative, the Bell basis measurements performed subsequently are not, as they involve basis states (|00⟩−|11⟩)/2(\left|00\right\rangle-\left|11\right\rangle)/\sqrt{2} and (|01⟩−|10⟩)/2(\left|01\right\rangle-\left|10\right\rangle)/\sqrt{2}. In fact, the only sign-free measurement basis in this setting is the product basis {|00⟩,|01⟩,|10⟩,|11⟩}\{\left|00\right\rangle,\left|01\right\rangle,\left|10\right\rangle,\left|11\right\rangle\} which does not produce any entanglement.

More generally, it has been shown [32] that when an nn-qubit state |ψ⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle prepared by a constant depth 1D quantum circuit is non-negative, then the conditional correlations between two subsystems 𝖠\mathsf{A} and 𝖢\mathsf{C} upon measuring the rest of the system 𝖡=[n]∖𝖠∪𝖢\mathsf{B}=[n]\setminus{\mathsf{A}}\cup\mathsf{C} decay super-polynomially with the distance.

Non-negative stabilizer states (also known as CSS codes) are another family of states whose conditional correlations have been studied. Depending on their geometry, these states can host long-range topological order (e.g., the toric code). The limitations of neural networks in efficiently learning these states has been explored before in [37]. However, when such a state is the unique ground state of a local (stabilizer) Hamiltonian, it exhibits short-range conditional correlations [46]. It is also known that in the ground state of a stoquastic frustration-free Hamiltonian, the ratio between amplitudes ⟨y|ψ⟩⟨x|ψ⟩\frac{\left\langle y\middle|\psi\right\rangle}{\left\langle x\middle|\psi\right\rangle} can be efficiently computed when ⟨x|ψ⟩>0\left\langle x\middle|\psi\right\rangle>0 and ⟨y|H|x⟩<0\left\langle y\right|H\left|x\right\rangle<0 [14]. This property has been further extended to the class of ‘magic ratio’ Hamiltonians in [13].

In addition to these cases, we also numerically investigate the link between the sign structure of the amplitudes and conditional correlations. In Figure 4, we consider two families of tensor network states: matrix product states (MPS) and projected entangled pair states (PEPS). The amplitudes of these states are obtained by contracting the network of tensors. The sign structure in such tensor networks and its connection to efficient contraction algorithms has been recently studied in [20, 42]. Here, we investigate this connection from the viewpoint of conditional correlations. The (real) entries in each tensor are shifted Gaussian variables 𝒩⁡(μ,σ)\mathcal{N(\mu,\sigma)} with mean μ≥0\mu\geq 0 and variance σ2=1\sigma^{2}=1. By tuning the mean parameter μ\mu, we can change the sign structure of the corresponding amplitudes ψ⁡(x)\psi(x). When μ\mu becomes comparable to σ\sigma, the distribution of tensor entries shifts sufficiently into the positive region, resulting in amplitudes that are overwhelmingly positive, while choosing μ≃0\mu\simeq 0 generates states with varying signs. For a fixed mean value μ>0\mu>0, the percentage of strictly positive amplitudes ψ⁡(x)>0\psi(x)>0 increases with the bond dimension rr due to the concentration effects. When μ≃0\mu\simeq 0, increasing the bond dimension—thereby increasing entanglement—causes the conditional correlations to decay more slowly. This effect is particularly pronounced in random PEPS, where, beyond a bond dimension of 22, the CMI does not decay with high probability when μ≃0\mu\simeq 0. Conversely, in the μ≫0\mu\gg 0 regime, increasing the bond dimension eventually leads to shorter-range conditional correlations, as the majority of amplitudes become positive. These results are illustrated in Figure 4. As a result of Theorem II.2 such states with short-range conditional correlations admit an efficient neural network representation.

Next, we show an intriguing relation between the conditional independence and the entanglement entropy area law for sign-free quantum states. We note that the conditional independence studied so far is an information-theoretic property of the probability distribution obtained from measuring the state. The area law, however, is a bound satisfied by the von Neumann entropy of the reduced states. The sign-free assumption allows us to relate these classical and quantum information theoretic notions.

Theorem II.4 (Approximate conditional independence implies area law).

Consider an nn-qudit sign-free state |ψ⟩∈ℂd⊗⋯⊗ℂd\left|\psi\right\rangle\in\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathbb{C}^{d} on a lattice. Suppose the measurement distribution of this state satisfies the approximate conditional independence property (4) for a given tripartition 𝖠∪𝖡∪𝖢=[n]\mathsf{A}\cup\mathsf{B}\cup\mathsf{C}=[n] of the lattice such that 𝖠∩𝖢=∅\mathsf{A}\cap\mathsf{C}=\emptyset. The von Neumann entropy of the reduced state ρ𝖠\rho_{\mathsf{A}} in region 𝖠\mathsf{A} is upper bounded by

S⁡(ρ𝖠)=𝒪⁡(|𝖡|),S(\rho_{\mathsf{A}})=\mathcal{O}(|\mathsf{B}|),

which (up to log⁡(|𝖠|)\log(|\mathsf{A}|) factors) implies an area law S⁡(ρ𝖠)=𝒪⁡(|∂𝖠|⋅log⁡(|∂𝖠|))S(\rho_{\mathsf{A}})=\mathcal{O}(|\partial\mathsf{A}|\cdot\log(|\partial\mathsf{A}|)).

The proof of this theorem is stated in Appendix C. The additional log⁡(|∂𝖠|)\log(|\partial\mathsf{A}|) factor in the area law arises because controlling the error in applying the conditional independence property requires the distance between regions 𝖠\mathsf{A} and 𝖢\mathsf{C} (and thus the width of region 𝖡\mathsf{B}) to satisfy dist⁡(𝖠,𝖢)=𝒪⁡(log⁡(|𝖠|))\operatorname{dist}(\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C})=\mathcal{O}(\log(|\mathsf{A}|)). As a result, the size of region 𝖡\mathsf{B} is bounded by |𝖡|=𝒪⁡(|∂𝖠|⋅log⁡(|𝖠|))|\mathsf{B}|=\mathcal{O}(|\partial\mathsf{A}|\cdot\log(|\mathsf{A}|)). The area law scaling of entanglement entropy in gapped ground states has been associated with the existence of efficient tensor network representations for these states [5, 3, 2, 4]. Consequently, Theorem II.4 establishes a link between accurate representations of quantum states using neural networks and tensor networks.

II.3 Numerical simulations for prototypical spin systems

In Figure 5, we examine the decay rate of conditional mutual information (4) for some typical local Hamiltonians of interest: 1D transverse-field Ising model (TFIM), Heisenberg ladder Hamiltonian, and Rydberg atoms on a 2D lattice. For each case, a choice of regions 𝖠\mathsf{A}, 𝖡\mathsf{B}, and 𝖢\mathsf{C} is depicted in Figure 5, with region BB made larger in a natural way to change dist⁡(𝖠,𝖢)\mathrm{dist}(\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C}). Among these, the 1D TFIM and the Rydberg Hamiltonian are sign-free. All three Hamiltonians are gapped, have a unique ground state, and are studied in their disordered phase. By tuning a parameter of each Hamiltonian, we vary the spectral gap and observe that the conditional mutual information decays exponentially with distance. However, the decay rate slows as the spectral gap decreases and the system approaches the phase transition point.

III Long-range conditional correlations

III.1 Rotated cluster state

In this section, we consider quantum states whose measurement distribution exhibits long-range conditional correlations. The presence of these correlations is not necessarily an obstacle to the existence of efficient neural representations for the state. However, we show that such long-range correlations can affect the computational performance of conventional ML algorithms that aim to variationally find a neural representation of the state. To see this, we consider an nn-qubit state on a one-dimensional chain, which is the ground state of

HES=\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{ES}}= −∑k=2n−2Xk−1ZkXk+1\displaystyle-\sum_{k=2}^{n-2}X_{k-1}Z_{k}X_{k+1}
−Z1​X2−Xn−1​Xn−Xn−2​Zn−1​Zn.\displaystyle-Z_{1}X_{2}-X_{n-1}X_{n}-X_{n-2}Z_{n-1}Z_{n}. (9)

Up to Hadamard gates applied on all but the nn-th qubit, this Hamiltonian is equivalent to the Hamiltonian for the 1D cluster state. The ground state of HESH_{\mathrm{ES}} can be prepared using a depth-2 quantum circuit shown in Figure 6 that corresponds to the entanglement swapping (ES) setup in Figure 3. Specifically, a series of EPR pairs are first created and then transformed into the Bell basis. Consequently, the measurement distribution of this state in the computational basis exhibits long-range conditional correlations. However, these correlations change when a local basis transformation, given by a yy-rotation on each qubit, is applied. As stated in the following theorem, the resulting state—referred to as the rotated cluster state—exhibits conditional correlations that decay at a rate determined by the rotation angle.

Theorem III.1 (Decay of CMI in rotated cluster state).

Consider the ground state of the Hamiltonian in (9) for an even nn. Apply a yy-rotation Ry​(θ)=cos⁡(θ)⋅𝟙+i​sin⁡(θ)⋅YR_{y}(\theta)=\cos(\theta)\cdot\mathds{1}+i\sin(\theta)\cdot Y for θ∈[0,π/2]\theta\in[0,\pi/2] to each qubit and proceed to measure all qubits in the standard ZZ basis. Let 𝖠\mathsf{A}, 𝖢\mathsf{C}, and 𝖡\mathsf{B} represent the first qubit, the last qubit, and the remaining qubits, respectively. The conditional mutual information I(𝖠:𝖢|𝖡)I(\mathsf{A}:\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}) of the resulting measurement distribution satisfies

I(𝖠:𝖢|𝖡)≤cos(θ)n−2.\displaystyle I(\mathsf{A}:\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B})\leq\cos(\theta)^{n-2}. (10)

The proof of this theorem is provided in Section D.5. While (10) provides a provable upper bound on conditional correlations, Figure 6(b) presents numerically simulated values of I(𝖠:𝖢|𝖡)I(\mathsf{A}:\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B}) for varying angles θ\theta, confirming that the conditional correlation length increases as θ→0\theta\rightarrow 0.

The rotated cluster state admits an efficient neural network representation. This follows from the fact that this state has a matrix product representation with bond dimension r=2r=2, which can be directly mapped to a recurrent neural network. An explicit construction of such a mapping is given in [73] and a general correspondence between tensor network states and neural quantum states can be found in [61]. Starting from a matrix product state with bond dimension rr, the resulting RNN consists of hidden memories hk∈ℂrh_{k}\in\mathbb{C}^{r} and cells that output conditional probabilities and complex phases by computing a weighted norm and affine map of hkh_{k}.

Despite the existence of an efficient RNN representation for the rotated 1D cluster state, we show that variationally finding this representation for small rotation angles with long-range conditional correlations could be computationally difficult. We employ Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) algorithm reviewed in Section A.2 for this task. This algorithm solves the optimization problem minw⟨ψw|H|ψw⟩\min_{w}\left\langle\psi_{w}\right|H\left|\psi_{w}\right\rangle over a set of trial states, which in this case is a family of neural quantum states |ψ⟩w\left|\psi\right\rangle_{w}, each with a set of weights denoted by ww. Granted we can query the amplitudes ⟨x|ψw⟩\left\langle x\middle|\psi_{w}\right\rangle and sample from |⟨x|ψw⟩|2\lvert\left\langle x\middle|\psi_{w}\right\rangle\rvert^{2}, the energy ⟨ψw|H|ψw⟩\left\langle\psi_{w}\right|H\left|\psi_{w}\right\rangle can be efficiently evaluated. Additionally, if the neural quantum states are expressive enough with a favorable optimization landscape, the estimated energy minw⟨ψw|H|ψw⟩\min_{w}\left\langle\psi_{w}\right|H\left|\psi_{w}\right\rangle can closely approximate the ground state energy of the local Hamiltonian HH.

We apply VMC to the rotated cluster state Hamiltonian (9) over 6464 qubits with two choices of neural networks as our variational ansatz: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) [34] and Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM) [17]. Our numerical findings are summarized in Figure 6 and described in more detail in Appendix E. We observe that, in general and for both architectures, as θ→0\theta\to 0 and longer-range conditional correlations form, the performance of VMC degrades almost monotonically. This suggests that conventional optimization schemes may struggle to find the neural representation of simple classes of states with long-range conditional correlations. Similar difficulties in learning long-term dependencies in recurrent networks using gradient descent are well-known in machine learning [8].

The longer-range correlations for smaller values of θ\theta arise due to changes in both the magnitudes and phases of the probability amplitudes ψ⁡(x)\psi(x). As discussed in Section II.2, the emergence of a complex phase structure is likely necessary for the development of these longer-range correlations. To what extent does the performance degradation of VMC, observed in Figure 6 for the rotated cluster state, result from changes in the complex phases ψ⁡(x)/|ψ⁡(x)|\psi(x)/|\psi(x)| versus the magnitudes |ψ⁡(x)||\psi(x)|? Indeed, complex phases are known to pose significant challenges for training neural quantum states with VMC or in quantum tomography applications [56, 25, 65, 15].

To address this, we first exactly determine the phases ψ⁡(x)/|ψ⁡(x)|\psi(x)/|\psi(x)| in the rotated cluster state. We then provide these phases as input to VMC, training the neural network solely to learn the magnitudes |ψ⁡(x)||\psi(x)| of the state. The results shown in Figure 6(c)-(d) indicate that the performance of VMC improves and achieves a more accurate approximation of the ground state energy except in the vicinity of θ=0\theta=0, although the relative error and training steps required still increase as θ\theta decreases. In the vicinity of θ=0\theta=0, VMC does not converge to the ground state even when the phases are known, underscoring the challenge of training the magnitudes |ψ⁡(x)||\psi(x)| in regimes with long-range conditional correlations. While having the phases improves VMC’s performance, determining these phases or finding a local change of basis to remove them in general systems is computationally challenging [30].

III.2 Higher dimensions

The 1D rotated cluster state serves as an example of a state with long-range conditional correlations, where the conditional probabilities p⁡(xk∣x1,…,xk−1)p(x_{k}\mid x_{1},\dots,x_{k-1}) are simple functions of their inputs and can be efficiently represented using neural networks. Such correlations have also been observed in higher-dimensional variants of this state, such as 2D graph states [47].

Beyond these structured states, how prevalent are long-range conditional correlations in physically relevant quantum states, and do their conditional probabilities p⁡(xk|x1,…,xk−1)p(x_{k}|x_{1},\dots,x_{k-1}) easily admit efficient neural representation? Here we present evidence from a series of recent works that suggest certain random ensembles of states possess long-range conditional correlations with conditional probabilities p⁡(xk|x1,…,xk−1)p(x_{k}|x_{1},\dots,x_{k-1}) which are complex functions not easily representable with neural networks.

Consider states generated by random ensembles of shallow geometrically-local quantum circuits or tensor networks with small bond dimension in two- or higher-dimensional lattices. As discussed in Section II.1, such states are believed to undergo a phase transition beyond a certain critical depth d∗d^{*} or bond dimension r∗r^{*} where the conditional correlations transition from short-range to long-range with high probability. In these examples, the critical depth d∗d^{*} and the bond dimension r∗r^{*} are small constants independent of the number of qubits. For instance, numerical simulations in 2D random circuits with the brickwork architecture suggest d∗=6d^{*}=6 [7, 6, 54], while for random PEPS, the critical bond dimension may be as small as r∗=2r^{*}=2 [44, 28]. Although a rigorous proof of these phase transitions is still lacking, recent work [7] shows that random 2D shallow quantum circuits satisfying a notion of anti-concentration—believed to occur at depths ≥Ω⁡(log⁡(n))\geq\Omega(\log(n)) for the brickwork architecture—exhibit long-range conditional correlations. This can, in fact, be unconditionally proven for a depth-22 “coarse-grained” circuit architecture composed of random gates acting on 𝒪⁡(log⁡(n))\mathcal{O}(\log(n)) qubits. This was further improved in recent work [49], which proves that certain random quantum circuit architectures generate long-range conditional correlations at constant depth and fixed qudit dimension.

The presence of long-range conditional correlations in the output states of random 2D shallow random circuits or tensor network states poses a challenge to accurately represent these states with neural networks. Here, we explore evidence for this from previous works. Mapping the tensor network representation of these states to a neural network, as we previously did for the 1D cluster state, does not immediately apply here due to the difficulty of contracting the corresponding 2D tensor networks [54, 28]. Moreover, the intricate patterns of multipartite measurement-induced entanglement, which non-locally appear everywhere in such randomly generated states [7, 6, 54], suggest that the conditional probabilities p⁡(xk|x1,…,xk−1)p(x_{k}|x_{1},\dots,x_{k-1}) are likely complex functions of their inputs x1,…,xkx_{1},\dots,x_{k}. Focusing on recurrent neural networks, this suggests that deeper feedforward neural networks in RNN cells are required to compute these complex dependencies. Additionally, the dimension of the hidden state vectors hkh_{k} must scale as Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) with the number of qubits to retain the information of previous variables x1,…,xk−1x_{1},\dots,x_{k-1} for k∈[n]k\in[n].

The complexity introduced by these long-range entanglement patterns has been further investigated in [7], where the authors provide formal evidence that classical probabilistic circuits whose depth grows sub-logarithmically with nn cannot simulate the output distribution p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) of random 2D shallow quantum circuits given a description of the quantum circuit as input. In fact, it is conjectured [54] that this limitation extends to any polynomial-time classical algorithm. There are also complexity theory barriers to the very precise computation of the output probabilities p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) of random shallow circuits. In particular, it is known that achieving additive errors of 2−Ω⁡(n2)2^{-\Omega(n^{2})} is #𝖯\mathsf{P}-hard [53, 9]. Finally, the worst-case complexity of estimating the ground state energy of local Hamiltonians, whose ground state amplitudes admit a succinct representation (e.g., via classical neural networks) is shown to be MA\mathrm{MA}-complete [41], where MA\mathrm{MA} is a randomized extension of the complexity class NP\mathrm{NP}.

IV Outlook

Our work provides evidence that the performance of neural network representation of quantum states depends on the amount of conditional correlations in the state’s measurement distribution. Our results raise several intriguing open questions, some of which are briefly highlighted below.

Probability amplitudes with non-trivial phases:

We examined the expressive power of classical neural networks in capturing the magnitudes |ψ⁡(x)||\psi(x)| of probability amplitudes, leaving the complex phases ψ⁡(x)/|ψ⁡(x)|\psi(x)/|\psi(x)| mostly unaddressed. What structures might these complex phases assume in physically relevant states, such as the ground states of local Hamiltonians? It is known that not all these complex phases can be removed by a local change of basis, and when present, they degrade the performance of neural quantum states in learning and simulation tasks [56, 25, 65, 15]. In connection with this, we might ask whether the unique ground state of any gapped, sign-free local Hamiltonian exhibits short-range conditional correlations, or if there exist concrete counterexamples. Resolving this question is tied to understanding the performance of Variational Monte Carlo (VMC). VMC avoids the sign problem by sampling directly from a parametrized wavefunction, rather than from high-dimensional path integrals or density matrices, as in quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, while the sign problem is not apparent in VMC’s construction, it might still implicitly encounter similar challenges due to limitations in efficiently representing the wavefunction.

Gapless phases and power-law interactions:

Our analysis of conditional correlations focused on gapped local Hamiltonians. What is the nature of these correlations near critical points, in gapless phases, or when interactions are not strictly local but instead decay with distance according to a power law?

Practical performance with long-range conditional correlations:

In two- and higher-dimensional lattices, states prepared by random quantum circuits or tensor networks likely exhibit long-range conditional correlations, even at shallow depths or small bond dimensions. While this suggests that precise neural representations of such states may be inefficient, the impact on practical applications, which often rely on coarser approximations and pertain to more structured states, remains unclear. Can the performance of neural quantum states in representing long-range correlations be enhanced by increasing network parameters or designing tailored architectures, thereby improving on the methods in Figure 6?

Other neural network architectures:

Modern architectures such as Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV) [57] and Transformer Quantum State (TQS) [64] are equipped with a self-attention mechanism designed to better capture long-range correlations in speech or language modeling. Thus, one might hope that using them to solve the ground state problem with long-range correlations could lead to improved performance. Our preliminary numerical simulations show that, with a limited number of parameters, these networks exhibit similar performance degradation in the presence of long-range conditional correlations. A more thorough investigation of these architectures is left for future work.

Appendix A Preliminaries

A.1 Architectures of neural quantum states

Neural networks can succinctly represent an nn-qubit quantum state |ψ⟩=∑x∈{0,1}nψ(x)|x⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\psi(x)\left|x\right\rangle in the computational basis {|x⟩:x∈{0,1}n}\{\left|x\right\rangle:x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\} by encoding the complex amplitudes ψ⁡(x)∈ℂ\psi(x)\in\mathbb{C}. We denote the quantum state parametrized by neural network weights ww as |ψw⟩\left|\psi_{w}\right\rangle. When the context is clear, we may omit the dependence on ww. This, for instance, can be achieved by specifying the squared-magnitude p⁡(x)p(x) and the phase g⁡(x)g(x) parts of each amplitude ⟨x|ψ⟩=p⁡(x)​ei​g​(x)\left\langle x\middle|\psi\right\rangle=\sqrt{p(x)}e^{ig(x)} or the real Re⁡(ψ⁡(x))\operatorname{Re}(\psi(x)) and imaginary Im⁡(ψ⁡(x))\operatorname{Im}(\psi(x)) components. Alternatively, the network may directly output ψ⁡(x)\psi(x) by allowing complex-valued neurons or using architectures such as complex-valued restricted Boltzmann machines [17]. We primarily focus on the case of polar representation in terms of functions p⁡(x)p(x) and g⁡(x)g(x) using real weights ww for a clearer exposition.

Feedforward neural networks: The first neural network architecture we consider is the feedforward network, shown in Figure 1. Such a network consists of a series of layers including input, hidden, and output layers. The depth of the neural network refers to the number of layers LL after the input layer. Each layer i∈[L]i\in[L] consists of nin_{i} neurons which are connected to the following layer with certain weights. The maximum number of neurons over all layers W=maxi∈[L]⁡niW=\max_{i\in[L]}n_{i} is known as the width of the network. The neuron located at position j∈[ni]j\in[n_{i}] within layer i∈[L]i\in[L] operates by transforming the input vector z∈ℝni−1z\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i-1}}, through a function consisting of two main components: an affine transformation characterized by ⟨wi​j|z⟩+bi​j\langle w_{ij}|z\rangle+b_{ij}, where the vector wi​j∈ℝni−1w_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i-1}} and the scalar bi​j∈ℝb_{ij}\in\mathbb{R} represent the weight and bias parameters, respectively; and also, a nonlinear transformation by the activation function σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot). Common choices for σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) include the rectified linear unit (ReLU), defined as z→max⁡(0,z)z\rightarrow\max(0,z), and the sigmoid function, given by z→11+e−zz\rightarrow\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}. Together, these elements enable the neuron to perform complex mappings from inputs to outputs, contributing to the neural network’s ability to model nonlinear relationships.

Recurrent neural networks: A probability distribution p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) can be expressed using its conditional distributions by

p(x1,…,xn)=p(x1)p(x2|x1)⋯p(xn|x1,…,xn−1).\displaystyle p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=p(x_{1})p(x_{2}|x_{1})\cdots p(x_{n}|x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}). (11)

A recurrent neural network, shown in Figure 1, consists of nn recurrent cells. The cell i∈[n]i\in[n] takes as input a hidden variable hi−1∈ℝni−1h_{i-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i-1}} and the binary value xi−1∈{0,1}x_{i-1}\in\{0,1\} (with h0h_{0} and x0x_{0} some fixed constant values). The output of the cell is an updated hidden variable hi∈ℝnih_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{i}} given by hi=fh​(xi−1,hi−1)h_{i}=f_{h}(x_{i-1},h_{i-1}) and a binary probability distribution given by fp​(hi)∈ℝ2f_{p}(h_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. Here, fh​(⋅)f_{h}(\cdot) and fp​(⋅)f_{p}(\cdot) are functions composing an affine and a non-linear activation maps similar to the neurons in the feedforward neural network.

The distributions generated by each recurrent cell is used to specify the conditional distribution p⁡(xi|x1,…,xi−1)=fp​(hi)p(x_{i}|x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1})=f_{p}(h_{i}). This along with the conditional form in (11) can be used to directly sample from the distribution p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}), a feature known as the autoregressive property. This is achieved by first sampling 𝒙𝟏∼p⁡(x1)\bm{x_{1}}\sim p(x_{1}) using the output of the first recurrent cell in the network. Next, the sampled 𝒙𝟏\bm{x_{1}} is given as input to the second recurrent cell whose output value is used to sample 𝒙𝟐∼p⁡(x2|x1)\bm{x_{2}}\sim p(x_{2}|x_{1}). Continuing this way, we end by sampling 𝒙𝒏∼p⁡(xn|x1,…,xn−1)\bm{x_{n}}\sim p(x_{n}|x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}). The conditional distributions in each step can be efficiently evaluated and a binary value is sampled consequently. This renders the overall sampling 𝒙𝟏,…,𝒙𝒏∼p⁡(x1,…,xn)\bm{x_{1}},\dots,\bm{x_{n}}\sim p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) efficient, contrasting with the exponential cost of sampling a general multivariate distribution. Such networks define recurrent neural network wavefunctions by expressing the measurement distribution p⁡(x)p(x) of a quantum state ∑x∈{0,1}np⁡(x)​ei​g​(x)\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\sqrt{p(x)}e^{ig(x)} [34, 35]. Extensions of this architecture for generating the phase components g⁡(x)g(x) have been also considered [34].

Restricted Boltzmann machines: In this case, the network features a visible and a single hidden layer of neurons. The visible layer has nn nodes taking values x=(x1,…,xn)∈{0,1}nx=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n} that specify the computational basis as before. The nhn_{h} neurons in the hidden layer are binary-valued and fully connected to those in the visible layer by complex weights {wi​j}i∈[n],j∈[nh]\{w_{ij}\}_{i\in[n],j\in[n_{h}]}. The visible and hidden neurons also admit complex weights {ai}i∈[n]\{a_{i}\}_{i\in[n]} and {bj}j∈[nh]\{b_{j}\}_{j\in[n_{h}]}. The expressivity of this architecture can be controlled by adjusting the number of hidden neurons nhn_{h}. The output of the network with weights w=∪i​j{wi​j,ai,bj}w=\cup_{ij}\{w_{ij},a_{i},b_{j}\} is the un-normalized complex amplitudes ψw​(x)\psi_{w}(x) given by

ψw​(x)\displaystyle\psi_{w}(x) =∑y∈{0,1}ne∑i,jwi​j​xi​yj+∑iai​xi+∑jbj​yj\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{n}}e^{\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}x_{i}y_{j}+\sum_{i}a_{i}x_{i}+\sum_{j}b_{j}y_{j}}
=∏j∈[nh](1+ebj+∑iwi​j​xi)⋅e∑iai​xi\displaystyle=\prod_{j\in[n_{h}]}(1+e^{b_{j}+\sum_{i}w_{ij}x_{i}})\cdot e^{\sum_{i}a_{i}x_{i}} (12)

We see from (12) that for a bounded number of hidden neurons nh=poly⁡(n)n_{h}=\operatorname{poly}(n), the output of the network can be efficiently evaluated. This is in contrast to the deeper version of these networks, featuring multiple hidden layers, where computing their output may become computationally intractable. Despite their simple structures, restricted Boltzmann machines can efficiently express a variety of quantum states [17, 27, 48] and are conventionally used in the Monte Carlo simulations of ground state properties [17, 50].

A.2 Review of variational Monte Carlo

Neural quantum states offer a computationally powerful model that can be used to find the ground state properties of quantum systems. The underlying idea is that the ground state of an interacting quantum system described by a Hamiltonian HH can be approximately found by solving the variational problem minw⟨ψw|H|ψw⟩\min_{w}\ \left\langle\psi_{w}\right|H\left|\psi_{w}\right\rangle, where the energy of a family of neural quantum states |ψw⟩\left|\psi_{w}\right\rangle is minimized over their set of weights ww. It is not hard to see that an equivalent expression for this minimization is given by

minw⟨ψw|H|ψw⟩=minw𝔼𝒙∼|ψw​(x)|2(∑x′⟨𝒙|H|x′⟩⋅ψw​(x′)ψw​(𝒙))⏟=:ℰlocal​(𝒙).\displaystyle\min_{w}\ \left\langle\psi_{w}\right|H\left|\psi_{w}\right\rangle=\min_{w}\mathbb{E\/}_{\bm{x}\sim|\psi_{w}(x)|^{2}}\underbrace{\left(\sum_{x^{\prime}}\left\langle\bm{x}\right|H|x^{\prime}\rangle\cdot\frac{\psi_{w}(x^{\prime})}{\psi_{w}(\bm{x})}\right)}_{=:\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{local}}(\bm{x})}. (13)

The resulting optimization algorithm is known as the variational Monte Carlo (VMC) and has been applied in a series of recent works to find precise estimates of the ground state properties. For the objective function in minimizaiton (13) to be computable in poly⁡(n)\operatorname{poly}(n) time, one needs

  • (1)

    the term ℰlocal​(𝒙)\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{local}}(\bm{x}), known as the local energy, to be bounded and can be efficiently evaluated,

  • (2)

    an algorithm that efficiently draws samples 𝒙\bm{x} from the measurement distribution |ψw​(x)|2|\psi_{w}(x)|^{2}.

The first condition is satisfied when HH is a local (or more generally a sparse) Hamiltonian and the amplitudes ψw​(x)\psi_{w}(x) can be computed in poly⁡(n)\operatorname{poly}(n) time up to a normalization factor, a property that is satisfied for neural quantum states. Assuming the efficient sampling in condition (2) can be satisfied as well, the objective function is estimated by taking the empirical average of many samples 𝒙𝟏,…,𝒙𝑻\bm{x_{1}},\dots,\bm{x_{T}} drawn independently from |ψw​(x)|2|\psi_{w}(x)|^{2} using Markov chain sampling algorithms such as Metropolis–Hastings [22, 12, 13] or autoregressive methods such as those used in recurrent neural networks [34]. One can estimate ⟨ψ|H|ψ⟩\left\langle\psi\right|H\left|\psi\right\rangle up to an error ϵ\epsilon with probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta using a total of T≤𝒪(⟨ψ|H2|ψ⟩/ϵ2)T\leq\mathcal{O}(\left\langle\psi\right|H^{2}\left|\psi\right\rangle/\epsilon^{2}) samples 𝒙∼|⟨x|ψ⟩|2\bm{x}\sim|\left\langle x\middle|\psi\right\rangle|^{2}. This follows from standard concentration results and the fact that the variance of the real and imaginary parts of local energy can be bounded by ⟨ψw|H2|ψw⟩≤||H2||\left\langle\psi_{w}\right|H^{2}\left|\psi_{w}\right\rangle\leq{|\hskip-1.59016pt|H^{2}|\hskip-1.59016pt|} (refer e.g. to [38] for a detailed derivation).

This leads to a stochastic optimization problem that can be solved using methods such as stochastic reconfiguration (or natural gradient descent) [63, 17]. The performance of variational Monte Carlo in finding the ground state is contingent upon the optimization landscape (13) over the set of weights ww. Crucially, for this approach to succeed, there must exist a set of weights w∗w^{*} such that the neural quantum state |ψw∗⟩\left|\psi_{w^{*}}\right\rangle approximately represents the true ground state. Addressing this issue of expressivity is the primary objective of this work.

Appendix B Decay of CMI Implies Efficient Representations

B.1 Shallow feedforward neural network (FNN) representation

In this section, we show that the magnitudes |ψ⁡(x)||\psi(x)| of the ground state amplitudes admit an approximate representation using shallow feedforward neural nets. We start with deriving a factorized form for the measurement distribution p⁡(x)=|ψ⁡(x)|2p(x)=|\psi(x)|^{2} assuming it satisfies the conditional independence property.

Theorem B.1.

Consider the setup of Theorem II.2 and suppose the measurement distribution p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) satisfies the approximate conditional independence property

I(𝖠:𝖢|𝖡)≤nc0⋅e−dist(𝖠,𝖢)/ξI(\mathsf{A}:\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B})\leq n^{c_{0}}\cdot e^{-\mathrm{dist}(\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C})/\xi}

as in Definition II.1 with some constant c0c_{0} and the CMI length ξ\xi. Fix parameters M=𝒪⁡(nℓ0DΛ⋅logDΛ⁡(n))M=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{n}{\ell_{0}^{D_{\Lambda}}\cdot\log^{D_{\Lambda}}(n)}\right) and s=𝒪⁡(ℓ0DΛ⋅logDΛ⁡(n))s=\mathcal{O}(\ell_{0}^{D_{\Lambda}}\cdot\log^{D_{\Lambda}}(n)). Then the distribution p⁡(x1,…,xn)p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) in its support can be approximately factored in its support as

∑x∈{0,1}n|p⁡(x)−∏k=1Mp⁡(xsk)∏k=1M−1p⁡(xsk′)|≤n−(ℓ0/ξ−c0−1).\displaystyle\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\left\lvert p(x)-\frac{\prod_{k=1}^{M}p(x_{s_{k}})}{\prod_{k=1}^{M-1}p(x_{s^{\prime}_{k}})}\right\rvert\leq n^{-(\ell_{0}/\xi-c_{0}-1)}. (14)

Here p⁡(xsk)p(x_{s_{k}}) and p⁡(xsk′)p(x_{s^{\prime}_{k}}) are marginal distributions over variables xskx_{s_{k}} and xsk′x_{s^{\prime}_{k}} supported on sk,sk′⊆[n]s_{k},s^{\prime}_{k}\subseteq[n] such that maxk∈[M]⁡|sk|≤s\max_{k\in[M]}|s_{k}|\leq s and maxk∈[M−1]⁡|sk′|≤s\max_{k\in[M-1]}|s^{\prime}_{k}|\leq s.

Proof.

We start with an equivalent formulation of the conditional independence property. For any three subsets 𝖠\mathsf{A},𝖡\mathsf{B}, and OPEN𝖢)\mathsf{C}) such that dist⁡(𝖠,𝖢)=2​ℓ0⋅log⁡(n)\mathrm{dist}(\mathsf{A},\mathsf{C})=2\ell_{0}\cdot\log(n) and p⁡(x𝖡)>0p(x_{\mathsf{B}})>0 we have

∑x𝖡p⁡(x𝖡)​∑x𝖠,x𝖢|p⁡(x𝖠,x𝖡,x𝖢)p⁡(x𝖡)−p⁡(x𝖠,x𝖡)p⁡(x𝖡)⋅p⁡(x𝖡,x𝖢)p⁡(x𝖡)|\displaystyle\sum_{x_{\mathsf{B}}}p(x_{\mathsf{B}})\sum_{x_{\mathsf{A}},x_{\mathsf{C}}}\left|\frac{p(x_{\mathsf{A}},x_{\mathsf{B}},x_{\mathsf{C}})}{p(x_{\mathsf{B}})}-\frac{p(x_{\mathsf{A}},x_{\mathsf{B}})}{p(x_{\mathsf{B}})}\cdot\frac{p(x_{\mathsf{B}},x_{\mathsf{C}})}{p(x_{\mathsf{B}})}\right| =𝔼𝖡​‖p𝖠,𝖢|𝖡−p𝖠|𝖡⊗p𝖢|𝖡‖1\displaystyle=\mathbb{E\/}_{\mathsf{B}}{|\hskip-1.59016pt|p_{{\mathsf{A}},{\mathsf{C}}|{\mathsf{B}}}-p_{{\mathsf{A}}|{\mathsf{B}}}\otimes p_{{\mathsf{C}}|{\mathsf{B}}}|\hskip-1.59016pt|}_{1}
≤2⋅I(𝖠:𝖢|𝖡)\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{2\cdot I(\mathsf{A}:\mathsf{C}|\mathsf{B})}
≤poly(|𝖠|,|𝖢|)⋅n−ℓ0/ξ\displaystyle\leq\operatorname{poly}(|\mathsf{A}|,|\mathsf{C}|)\cdot n^{-\ell_{0}/\xi}
≤n−(ℓ0/ξ−c0),\displaystyle\leq n^{-(\ell_{0}/\xi-c_{0})}, (15)

where the expectation is over 𝒙B∼p𝖡​(x𝖡)\bm{x}_{B}\sim p_{\mathsf{B}}(x_{\mathsf{B}}) and c0c_{0} is a suitable constant. Next, we are going to apply this bound repeatedly to factorize the measurement distribution p⁡(x)p(x).

One-dimensional chain:

We first consider the case when the qubits are arranged on an open chain with DΛ=1D_{\Lambda}=1. Divide the chain to contiguous sets 𝖠1,𝖠2,…,𝖠M\mathsf{A}_{1},\mathsf{A}_{2},\dots,\mathsf{A}_{M} where each |𝖠i|=2​ℓ0⋅log⁡(n)|\mathsf{A}_{i}|=2\ell_{0}\cdot\log(n). Replacing 𝖠=𝖠1\mathsf{A}=\mathsf{A}_{1}, 𝖡=𝖠2\mathsf{B}=\mathsf{A}_{2} and 𝖢=𝖠3,…,𝖠M\mathsf{C}=\mathsf{A}_{3},\dots,\mathsf{A}_{M} in bound (15) yields:

‖p𝖠1,𝖠2,…,𝖠M−p𝖠1,𝖠2⋅p𝖠2−1⋅p𝖠2,…,𝖠M‖1≤n−(ℓ0/ξ−c0)\displaystyle{\big|\hskip-1.59016pt\big|p_{\mathsf{A}_{1},\mathsf{A}_{2},\dots,\mathsf{A}_{M}}-p_{\mathsf{A}_{1},\mathsf{A}_{2}}\cdot p^{-1}_{\mathsf{A}_{2}}\cdot p_{\mathsf{A}_{2},\dots,\mathsf{A}_{M}}\big|\hskip-1.59016pt\big|}_{1}\leq n^{-(\ell_{0}/\xi-c_{0})} (16)

Similarly, we can apply (15) to the marginal distribution p𝖠2,…,𝖠Mp_{\mathsf{A}_{2},\dots,\mathsf{A}_{M}}. Continuing in this manner, in the kk’th step, we factorize p𝖠k,…,𝖠Mp_{\mathsf{A}_{k},\dots,\mathsf{A}_{M}} to

‖p𝖠k,…,𝖠M−p𝖠k,𝖠k+1⋅p𝖠k+1−1⋅p𝖠k+1,…,𝖠M‖1≤n−(ℓ0/ξ−c0)\displaystyle{\big|\hskip-1.59016pt\big|p_{\mathsf{A}_{k},\dots,\mathsf{A}_{M}}-p_{\mathsf{A}_{k},\mathsf{A}_{k+1}}\cdot p^{-1}_{\mathsf{A}_{k+1}}\cdot p_{\mathsf{A}_{k+1},\dots,\mathsf{A}_{M}}\big|\hskip-1.59016pt\big|}_{1}\leq n^{-(\ell_{0}/\xi-c_{0})} (17)

||p𝖠1,…,𝖠M−∏k=1M−2p𝖠k,𝖠k+1p𝖠k+1⋅p𝖠M,𝖠M−1||1≤M⋅n−ℓ0/ξ≤n−(ℓ0/ξ−c0−1)\displaystyle{\left|\hskip-1.59016pt\left|p_{\mathsf{A}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{A}_{M}}-\prod_{k=1}^{M-2}\frac{p_{\mathsf{A}_{k},\mathsf{A}_{k+1}}}{p_{\mathsf{A}_{k+1}}}\cdot p_{\mathsf{A}_{M},\mathsf{A}_{M-1}}\right|\hskip-1.59016pt\right|}_{1}\leq M\cdot n^{-\ell_{0}/\xi}\leq n^{-(\ell_{0}/\xi-c_{0}-1)} (18)

We now move the more general case of a DΛD_{\Lambda}-dimensional lattice Λ\Lambda, which for simplicity, we assume is the cubic lattice ℤDΛ\mathbb{Z}^{D_{\Lambda}}. Suppose we divide the lattice into a collection of cubic subsets ∪k=1M𝖠k\cup_{k=1}^{M}\mathsf{A}_{k}, where each 𝖠k\mathsf{A}_{k} has side-length ℓ0⋅log⁡(n)\ell_{0}\cdot\log(n) and the total number of 𝖠k\mathsf{A}_{k} is M=⌈nℓ0DΛ⋅logDΛ⁡(n)⌉M=\lceil\frac{n}{\ell_{0}^{D_{\Lambda}}\cdot\log^{D_{\Lambda}}(n)}\rceil. Remark B.2.

The proof of Theorem B.1 for the one-dimensional systems, only requires a weaker version of the approximate conditional independence (4) where the sets 𝖠\mathsf{A}, 𝖡\mathsf{B}, and 𝖢\mathsf{C} are known to partition the whole chain, 𝖠∪𝖡∪𝖢=[n]\mathsf{A}\cup\mathsf{B}\cup\mathsf{C}=[n] (compared to applying (4) to subsets 𝖠∪𝖡∪𝖢⊂[n]\mathsf{A}\cup\mathsf{B}\cup\mathsf{C}\subset[n]). This is a consequence of the data processing inequality which implies that if the approximate conditional independence holds for a triparition 𝖠\mathsf{A}, 𝖡\mathsf{B}, and 𝖢\mathsf{C} where 𝖠=𝖠1∪𝖠2\mathsf{A}=\mathsf{A}_{1}\cup\mathsf{A}_{2}, then this property also holds for the subsets 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}, 𝖡\mathsf{B}, and 𝖢\mathsf{C}.

We show next that Theorem B.1 can be applied to construct a shallow neural network representation for the magnitude |ψ⁡(x)||\psi(x)| of the wavefunction amplitudes.

Theorem B.3 (Restatement of Theorem II.2).

Consider a local Hamiltonian on nn qubits with the ground state |ψ⟩=∑x∈{0,1}nψ(x)|x⟩\left|\psi\right\rangle=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\psi(x)\left|x\right\rangle defined on a DΛD_{\Lambda}-dimensional lattice Λ\Lambda with open boundary conditions. Suppose the measurement distribution p⁡(x)=|ψ⁡(x)|2p(x)=|\psi(x)|^{2} in this basis satisfies the approximate conditional independence property given in Definition II.1 with respect to geometrically contiguous regions shown in Figure 2. Then, there exists a feedforward neural network with

depth ​𝒪​(log⁡log⁡(n))​ and width ​n𝒪⁡(logDΛ−1⁡(n))\displaystyle\text{depth\ \ }\mathcal{O}\left(\log\log(n)\right)\text{ \ and width\ \ }n^{\mathcal{O}(\log^{D_{\Lambda}-1}(n))} (22)

that computes a function q⁡(x)q(x) such that ∑x|q⁡(x)−p⁡(x)|≤1/poly⁡(n)\sum_{x}|q(x)-p(x)|\leq 1/\operatorname{poly}(n). This can also be achieved using a recurrent neural network with DΛD_{\Lambda}-dimensional geometry, a memory size of 𝒪⁡(logDΛ⁡(n))\mathcal{O}(\log^{D_{\Lambda}}(n)), and feedforward cells with width and depth given by (22).

We postpone the proof of the second part to Section B.2 regarding the RNN representation to the next section and focus only on the feedforward representation in what follows.

Proof.

We give an explicit construction of a feedforward neural network that computes the factorization in Theorem B.1.

  1. 1.

    Any function q⁡(x1,…,xm):{0,1}m↦ℝq(x_{1},\dots,x_{m}):\{0,1\}^{m}\mapsto\mathbb{R} can be expressed by

    q⁡(x1,…,xm)=∑(y1,…,ym)∈{0,1}mq(y1,…,ym)⋅∏i=1mzi,yi​(xi),q(x_{1},\dots,x_{m})=\sum_{(y_{1},\dots,y_{m})\in\{0,1\}^{m}}q_{(y_{1},\dots,y_{m})}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}z_{i,y_{i}}(x_{i}),

    where we define zi,0​(xi)=1−xiz_{i,0}(x_{i})=1-x_{i} and zi,1​(xi)=xiz_{i,1}(x_{i})=x_{i} for each i∈[m]i\in[m]. Since the variables zi,yi∈{0,1}z_{i,y_{i}}\in\{0,1\}, we can multiply them exactly via the ReLU function σ⁡(x)=max⁡(0,x)\sigma(x)=\max(0,x). To see this, consider the sawtooth function [67, 74]:

    g⁡(x):=2⋅σ⁡(x)−4⋅σ⁡(x−12)+2⋅σ⁡(x−1).g(x):=2\cdot\sigma(x)-4\cdot\sigma(x-\frac{1}{2})+2\cdot\sigma(x-1).

    Define h⁡(x):=x−14⋅g⁡(x)h(x):=x-\frac{1}{4}\cdot g(x). This function satisfies h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0, h⁡(1/2)=1/4h(1/2)=1/4, and h⁡(1)=1h(1)=1. The connection between h⁡(x)h(x) and x⋅yx\cdot y for two Boolean variables is due to

    x⋅y=2⋅h⁡(x+y2)−x+y2.x\cdot y=2\cdot h(\frac{x+y}{2})-\frac{x+y}{2}.

    Multiple repetition of this network allows us to compute q⁡(x1,…,xm)q(x_{1},\dots,x_{m}) in depth 𝒪⁡(log⁡(m))\mathcal{O}(\log(m)) and width 𝒪⁡(2m)\mathcal{O}(2^{m}) with the coefficients q(y1,…,ym)q_{(y_{1},\dots,y_{m})} encoded in the weights of the network.

    Next, we apply the above construction to evaluate the expression (14) in Theorem B.1. That is, we can get

    log⁡(∏k=1Mp⁡(xsk)∏k=1M−1p⁡(xsk′))=∑k=1Mlog⁡(p⁡(xsk))−∑k=1M−1log⁡(p⁡(xxk′)).\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{\prod_{k=1}^{M}p(x_{s_{k}})}{\prod_{k=1}^{M-1}p(x_{s^{\prime}_{k}})}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{M}\log(p(x_{s_{k}}))-\sum_{k=1}^{M-1}\log(p(x_{x^{\prime}_{k}})). (23)

    by computing log⁡(p⁡(x𝗌k))\log(p(x_{\mathsf{s}_{k}})) for k∈[M]k\in[M] and log⁡(p⁡(x𝗌k′))\log(p(x_{\mathsf{s}^{\prime}_{k}})) for k∈[M−1]k\in[M-1] in parallel in depth 𝒪⁡(log⁡(s))\mathcal{O}(\log(s)) and width 𝒪⁡(M⋅2s)\mathcal{O}(M\cdot 2^{s}), where for a DΛD_{\Lambda}-dimensional lattice s=𝒪⁡(logDΛ⁡n)s=\mathcal{O}(\log^{D_{\Lambda}}{n}) and |𝗌k|,|𝗌k′′|≤s|\mathsf{s}_{k}|,|\mathsf{s}^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}}|\leq s. We assume the weights of the neurons are are encoded in 𝒪⁡(log⁡(n))\mathcal{O}(\log(n)) bits. Moreover, we can accommodate the cases when the value of a (possibly truncated) probability p⁡(x𝗌k)p(x_{\mathsf{s}_{k}}) is zero by including a constant positive offset in place of log⁡(p⁡(x𝗌k))\log(p(x_{\mathsf{s}_{k}})) and log⁡(p⁡(x𝗌k′))\log(p(x_{\mathsf{s}^{\prime}_{k}})).     depth ​𝒪​(log⁡log⁡(n))​ and width ​n𝒪⁡(logDΛ−1⁡(n))\displaystyle\text{depth\ \ }\mathcal{O}\left(\log\log(n)\right)\text{ \ and width\ \ }n^{\mathcal{O}(\log^{D_{\Lambda}-1}(n))} (24)

    that computes a function q⁡(x1,…,xn)q(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) such that

    ∑x1,…,xn|p⁡(x1,…,xn)−q⁡(x1,…,xn)|≤1poly⁡(n).\sum_{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}}\left|p(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})-q(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\right|\leq\frac{1}{\operatorname{poly}(n)}.
