D.6.4 Random shallow circuits

Now we consider unitaries 𝑼\bm{U} which originate from a 1D, low depth locally-random quantum circuits, as introduced in Section D.3.

Lemma D.20.

Fixed k≠k′,i∈[dD−1]k\neq k^{\prime},i\in[d^{D-1}], if 𝐔\bm{U} is drawn from the distribution described above,

𝔼𝑼​f​(𝑼,i,k,k′,σ𝖢)=(1(d2+1)​(d+1))D−1⋅tr⁡[σ𝖢2]≳1d3​D\mathbb{E\/}_{\bm{U}}f(\bm{U},i,k,k^{\prime},\sigma_{\mathsf{C}})=\left(\frac{1}{(d^{2}+1)(d+1)}\right)^{D-1}\cdot\operatorname{tr}[\sigma_{\mathsf{C}}^{2}]\gtrsim\frac{1}{d^{3D}} (92)
Proof.

Let us briefly high-level the proof of this claim. The key insight is two-fold: we picture the random quantum circuit in reverse, acting on the computational basis state |b⟩|b\rangle corresponding to the measurement outcome on BB. We view the action of the locally random quantum circuit as a linear combination of Identity and Swap operators, which evolve and mix in time; in particular, the dynamics of the (reverse time evolved) circuit can be understood through the domain walls between 𝟙\mathds{1} and SS regions on the 1D chain. To show the lower bound in the claim, we show that each domain wall adds a positive contribution to the expectation, and we pick a single domain wall trajectory to lower bound the total sum.

𝔼𝑼​[(𝑼𝖡𝖢†⊗𝑼𝖡′​𝖢′†)​(|i⟩​⟨i|𝖡⊗|i⟩​⟨i|𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′)​(𝑼𝖡𝖢⊗𝑼𝖡′​𝖢′)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E\/}_{\bm{U}}\bigg[(\bm{U}^{\dagger}_{\mathsf{BC}}\otimes\bm{U}^{\dagger}_{\mathsf{B^{\prime}C^{\prime}}})(|i\rangle\langle i|_{\mathsf{B}}\otimes|i\rangle\langle i|_{\mathsf{B}^{\prime}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}})(\bm{U}_{\mathsf{BC}}\otimes\bm{U}_{\mathsf{B^{\prime}C^{\prime}}})\bigg]
=𝔼𝑼,𝑾​[(𝑼𝖡𝖢†⊗𝑼𝖡′​𝖢′†)​(𝑾𝖡†⊗𝑾𝖡′†⋅|i⟩​⟨i|𝖡⊗|i⟩​⟨i|𝖡′⋅𝑾𝖡⊗𝑾𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′)​(𝑼𝖡𝖢⊗𝑼𝖡′​𝖢′)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E\/}_{\bm{U,\bm{W}}}\bigg[(\bm{U}^{\dagger}_{\mathsf{BC}}\otimes\bm{U}^{\dagger}_{\mathsf{B^{\prime}C^{\prime}}})(\bm{W}_{\mathsf{B}}^{\dagger}\otimes\bm{W}^{\dagger}_{\mathsf{B}^{\prime}}\cdot|i\rangle\langle i|_{\mathsf{B}}\otimes|i\rangle\langle i|_{\mathsf{B}^{\prime}}\cdot\bm{W}_{\mathsf{B}}\otimes\bm{W}_{\mathsf{B}^{\prime}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}})(\bm{U}_{\mathsf{BC}}\otimes\bm{U}_{\mathsf{B^{\prime}C^{\prime}}})\bigg]
=1dD−1​(d+1)D−1⋅∑γ1,…,γD−1∈{𝟙,SWAP}𝔼𝑼[(U𝖡𝖢†⊗U𝖡′​𝖢′†)(⊗i∈[D−1]γi⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′)(U𝖡𝖢⊗U𝖡′​𝖢′)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d^{D-1}(d+1)^{D-1}}\cdot\sum_{\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{D-1}\in\{\mathds{1},\operatorname{SWAP}\}}\mathbb{E\/}_{\bm{U}}\bigg[(U^{\dagger}_{\mathsf{BC}}\otimes U^{\dagger}_{\mathsf{B^{\prime}C^{\prime}}})(\otimes_{i\in[D-1]}\gamma_{i}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}})(U_{\mathsf{BC}}\otimes U_{\mathsf{B^{\prime}C^{\prime}}})\bigg] (93)

where we used the invariance property of Haar distribution of 𝑼\bm{U} under left multiplication by single qudit rotations, and applied the equality v. of Fact D.4. Each operator γi\gamma_{i} acts on a qudit in 𝖡\mathsf{B} and its corresponding copy in 𝖡′\mathsf{B^{\prime}}.

When the expectation over the two-local gates in 𝑼\bm{U} is taken, we get a mixture of the operators 𝟙\mathds{1} and SWAP\operatorname{SWAP} following Fact D.4. The overall result is a linear combination over identity and swap operators given by

∑γ∈{𝟙,SWAP}×2​(D−1)cγ⋅γ\sum_{\gamma\in\{\mathds{1},\operatorname{SWAP}\}^{\times 2(D-1)}}c_{\gamma}\cdot\gamma

where as seen in properties i.-iv. of Fact D.4, the coefficients cγc_{\gamma} are non-negative. Here, γ=⊗i∈[2​(D−1)]γi\gamma=\otimes_{i\in[2(D-1)]}\gamma_{i} where each γi\gamma_{i} is supported on a qudit and its copy in 𝖡𝖡′\mathsf{BB^{\prime}} or 𝖢𝖢′\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}. A simple property of the Swap operator ensures that these coefficients cσc_{\sigma} give us a lower bound to the quantity of interest:

Fact D.5.

The swap operator has a positive expectation over product states. That is, for any two density matrices ρ𝖷,ρ𝖸\rho_{\mathsf{X}},\rho_{\mathsf{Y}}, tr⁡(SWAP𝖷𝖸⋅ρ𝖷⊗ρ𝖸)≥0\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{XY}}\cdot\rho_{\mathsf{X}}\otimes\rho_{\mathsf{Y}})\geq 0.

By applying this bound we get

𝔼𝑼​f​(𝑼,i,k,k′,σ𝖢)\displaystyle\mathbb{E\/}_{\bm{U}}f(\bm{U},i,k,k^{\prime},\sigma_{\mathsf{C}}) =∑γ∈{𝟙,SWAP}×2​(D−1)cγ⋅tr⁡(γ⋅|k⟩​⟨k′|𝖡⊗|k′⟩​⟨k|𝖡′⊗σ𝖢⊗σ𝖢′)\displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in\{\mathds{1},\operatorname{SWAP}\}^{\times 2(D-1)}}c_{\gamma}\cdot\operatorname{tr}\left(\gamma\cdot|k\rangle\langle k^{\prime}|_{\mathsf{B}}\otimes|k^{\prime}\rangle\langle k|_{\mathsf{B^{\prime}}}\otimes\sigma_{\mathsf{C}}\otimes\sigma_{\mathsf{C^{\prime}}}\right)
=∑γ∈{𝟙,SWAP}×2​(D−1)cγ⋅tr⁡(γ⋅SWAP𝖡𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′⋅|k′⟩​⟨k′|𝖡⊗|k⟩​⟨k|𝖡′⊗σ𝖢⊗σ𝖢′)\displaystyle=\sum_{\gamma\in\{\mathds{1},\operatorname{SWAP}\}^{\times 2(D-1)}}c_{\gamma}\cdot\operatorname{tr}\left(\gamma\cdot\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}\cdot|k^{\prime}\rangle\langle k^{\prime}|_{\mathsf{B}}\otimes|k\rangle\langle k|_{\mathsf{B^{\prime}}}\otimes\sigma_{\mathsf{C}}\otimes\sigma_{\mathsf{C^{\prime}}}\right)
≥cSWAP𝖡𝖡′,𝟙𝖢𝖢′.\displaystyle\geq c_{\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}},\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}}. (94)

The last inequality holds since |k′⟩​⟨k′|𝖡⊗|k⟩​⟨k|𝖡′⊗σ𝖢⊗σ𝖢′|k^{\prime}\rangle\langle k^{\prime}|_{\mathsf{B}}\otimes|k\rangle\langle k|_{\mathsf{B^{\prime}}}\otimes\sigma_{\mathsf{C}}\otimes\sigma_{\mathsf{C^{\prime}}} is a density matrix over 𝖡,𝖡′,𝖢,𝖢′\mathsf{B},\mathsf{B^{\prime}},\mathsf{C},\mathsf{C^{\prime}} and a product state over 𝖡𝖢,𝖡′​𝖢′\mathsf{BC},\mathsf{B^{\prime}C^{\prime}}. Hence, from Fact D.5, we see that the summation in the second line includes non-negative terms. By choosing the term with γ=SWAP𝖡𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′\gamma=\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}, we obtain the stated lower bound in terms of cSWAP𝖡𝖡′,𝟙𝖢𝖢′c_{\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}},\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}}.

To conclude, we find a lower bound for the coefficient cSWAP𝖡𝖡′,𝟙𝖢𝖢′c_{\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}},\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}}. In the first place, as stated above, we apply a layer of single-qudit Haar random gates 𝑾𝖡\bm{W}_{\mathsf{B}} on subsystem 𝖡\mathsf{B} (and equivalently 𝖡′\mathsf{B^{\prime}}). This results in the coefficient corresponding to the operator SWAP𝖡𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}} possessing an initial weight 1dD−1​(d+1)D−1\frac{1}{d^{D-1}(d+1)^{D-1}}. Let qudit i0i_{0} (resp. i0+1i_{0}+1) be the boundary qudit of region 𝖡\mathsf{B} (resp. 𝖢\mathsf{C}). The link (i0,i0+1)(i_{0},i_{0}+1) marks the transition from SWAP\operatorname{SWAP} to 𝟙\mathds{1} in SWAP𝖡𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}, and is often called the ‘domain wall’. We next see how the transformation of SWAP𝖡𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}} due the application of the first level of two-qudit gates in 𝑼𝖡𝖢\bm{U}_{\mathsf{BC}} can be described by the movement of this domain wall. To this end, we divide this layer into three sets: 𝑼2†\bm{U}^{\dagger}_{2} denotes the gate acting on the boundary of 𝖡𝖢\mathsf{BC}, and 𝑼1†\bm{U}^{\dagger}_{1} and 𝑼3†\bm{U}^{\dagger}_{3} denote the set of gates acting only on 𝖡\mathsf{B} and 𝖢\mathsf{C}, respectively. We see from properties i. and ii. of Fact D.4 that

𝔼𝑼1(𝑼1†⊗2⋅SWAP𝖡𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′⋅𝑼1⊗2)=𝔼𝑼3(𝑼3†⊗2⋅SWAP𝖡𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′⋅𝑼3⊗2)=SWAP𝖡𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′.\mathbb{E\/}_{\bm{U}_{1}}\left(\bm{U}^{\dagger\otimes 2}_{1}\cdot\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}\cdot\bm{U}^{\otimes 2}_{1}\right)=\mathbb{E\/}_{\bm{U}_{3}}\left(\bm{U}^{\dagger\otimes 2}_{3}\cdot\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}\cdot\bm{U}^{\otimes 2}_{3}\right)=\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}.

Moving to the middle gates 𝑼2\bm{U}_{2}, the property iii. (or iv.) of Fact D.4 yields

𝔼𝑼2(𝑼2†⊗2⋅SWAPi0,i0′⊗𝟙i0+1,i0′+1⋅𝑼2⊗2)=dd2+1⋅(𝟙i0,i0′⊗𝟙i0+1,i0′+1+SWAPi0,i0′⊗SWAPi0+1,i0′+1).\mathbb{E\/}_{\bm{U}_{2}}\left(\bm{U}^{\dagger\otimes 2}_{2}\cdot\operatorname{SWAP}_{i_{0},i_{0}^{\prime}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{i_{0}+1,i^{\prime}_{0}+1}\cdot\bm{U}^{\otimes 2}_{2}\right)=\frac{d}{d^{2}+1}\cdot(\mathds{1}_{i_{0},i^{\prime}_{0}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{i_{0}+1,i^{\prime}_{0}+1}+\operatorname{SWAP}_{i_{0},i^{\prime}_{0}}\otimes\operatorname{SWAP}_{i_{0}+1,i^{\prime}_{0}+1}).

Combining these transformations, we see that the application of the first layer of gates on SWAP𝖡𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}, results in a linear combination of two operators such that the domain wall has moved to the left in one or to the right in the other. In expectation over the remaining layers of 𝑼\bm{U}, this domain wall propagates in time, resulting in a linear combination over operators that can be understood as a sum over domain wall trajectories.

Suppose the depth DD is odd so that the number of layers D−1D-1 in 𝑼\bm{U} is even. Let us consider the domain wall trajectory which starts and ends in the same place, resulting in the same operator SWAP𝖡𝖡′⊗𝟙𝖢𝖢′\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}}\otimes\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}. One such path is the trivial alternating path, where the domain wall steps between (i0,i0+1)(i_{0},i_{0}+1) and (i0+1,i0+2)(i_{0}+1,i_{0}+2) back and forth. By Fact D.4, at each step the coefficient of this path decays by a factor of dd2+1\frac{d}{d^{2}+1}, resulting in a contribution

cSWAP𝖡𝖡′,𝟙𝖢𝖢′\displaystyle c_{\operatorname{SWAP}_{\mathsf{BB^{\prime}}},\mathds{1}_{\mathsf{CC^{\prime}}}} ≥(1d⁡(d+1))D−1⋅(dd2+1)D−1≳1d3​D.\displaystyle\geq\left(\frac{1}{d(d+1)}\right)^{D-1}\cdot\left(\frac{d}{d^{2}+1}\right)^{D-1}\gtrsim\frac{1}{d^{3D}}.

∎

Appendix E Details of numerical simulations

For the RNN quantum states, both with and without phase information, we employ the tensor-gated recurrent unit (tensor-GRU) architecture [34] with a batch size of 256256. We utilize the Adam optimizer [43], setting the initial learning rate to 2×10−32\times 10^{-3}. The learning rate undergoes stepwise decays to 1×10−31\times 10^{-3} after 8,0008,000 iterations and to 4×10−44\times 10^{-4} after 24,00024,000 iterations. Each angle of the rotated cluster state is trained over a total of 10510^{5} iterations.

The RBM ansatz is implemented using the NetKet package [16, 71] with a batch size of 2122^{12}. Parameters are optimized through stochastic gradient descent (SGD) combined with stochastic reconfiguration (SR). The learning rate follows a warmup cosine decay schedule [24], starting at 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, increasing linearly to 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} by iteration 500500, and then decaying via a cosine curve to 2.5×10−42.5\times 10^{-4} by iteration 2,5002,500.

Finally, we investigate the conditional mutual information of random Matrix Product States (MPS) and Projected Entangled Pair States (PEPS) using Quimb [29]. Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) calculations are performed with ITensor Julia [26].

In addition to the plots presented in this paper, which focus on tensor-GRU and RBM architectures discussed in the main text, our code includes three additional experiments outlined below:

(1) We explore the RWKV ansatz [57] and the Transformer Quantum State (TQS) ansatz [64]. In our preliminary experiments, both architectures are trained with a batch size of 256256, using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4} with linear learning rate warmup from 10−610^{-6} for the first 10310^{3} steps. Both ansatz exhibit similar behaviors to tensor-GRU.

(2) Apart from the 1D rotated cluster state model with single-qubit Ry​(θ)R_{y}(\theta) rotations, we also observe similar connection between CMI correlation length and the performance of RNN quantum states for rotated graph state on a two-dimensional square lattice with: Hgraph=−∑1≤i≤N,1≤j≤NZi,j∏⟨(i,j),(k,l)⟩∈EXk,lH_{\text{graph}}=-\sum_{1\leq i\leq N,1\leq j\leq N}Z_{i,j}\prod_{\langle(i,j),(k,l)\rangle\in E}X_{k,l} where the subscript represents the location of the operator in the 2D-square lattice and EE is the set of all the edges of the 2D-square lattice.

(3) Inspired by the patched approach from [64], we modified the autoregressive output: instead of generating a two-fold probability distribution per qubit, the model produces a 2p2^{p}-fold probability distribution for pp qubits at each step. This modification reduces the effective depth of the autoregressive architecture at the cost of increasing the input and output dimensions at each step.
